questions.q: What is the fundamental constitutional difference between how the Prime Minister in India and the President in the USA assume office?
questions.a: The Indian Prime Minister is appointed by the President but must command a majority in the Lok Sabha (indirect election via legislature), while the US President is directly elected by the Electoral College for a fixed term. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are directly elected") reveals confusion between head of government and head of state roles, and ignorance of Article 75(3) on collective responsibility.

questions.q: Why can a parliamentary executive be removed more easily than a presidential executive? Explain using the concept of 'confidence of the house'.
questions.a: In a parliamentary system, the executive survives only while it enjoys the confidence of the lower house (Lok Sabha), expressed through a no-confidence motion (Article 75(3)); in a presidential system, the legislature cannot remove the executive except through impeachment for high crimes, a much higher threshold. A wrong answer (e.g., "both can be removed by legislature") misses the distinction between political accountability (confidence) and legal removal (impeachment).

questions.q: A country with a presidential system faces a legislature controlled by the opposition party. The President wants to pass a major reform bill. Analyze the likely outcome compared to a parliamentary system with the same party configuration.
questions.a: In the presidential system, the President cannot dissolve the legislature and must negotiate or use veto powers, often leading to gridlock; in a parliamentary system, the government would likely fall or call early elections, resolving the deadlock. A wrong answer (e.g., "both can dissolve legislature") confuses the separation of origin and survival in presidential systems with the fusion in parliamentary systems.

questions.q: Compare the role of the head of state in India (President) and the USA (President) across three dimensions: election method, executive powers, and accountability.
questions.a: India: indirectly elected (electoral college), ceremonial powers exercised on ministerial advice (Article 74), not personally accountable to Parliament. USA: directly elected (Electoral College), real executive powers, accountable via impeachment only. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are ceremonial") conflates head of state with head of government roles, ignoring that the US President combines both.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "A presidential system provides more stable government because the executive has a fixed term." Consider Indian coalition politics experience since 1989.
questions.a: Fixed terms prevent mid-term collapse but can create rigid gridlock when executive and legislature clash; India's parliamentary system allowed flexible coalition adjustments (1996-2014) but also saw frequent elections. Stability ≠ effectiveness. A wrong answer (e.g., "presidential is always better") ignores that stability without accountability can entrench unpopular governments, and parliamentary systems can be stable with single-party majorities.

questions.q: Draft a constitutional provision for a hybrid semi-presidential system (like France) for a hypothetical diverse federal country. Specify: how the President is elected, relationship with Prime Minister, and removal mechanisms.
questions.a: A good answer specifies: President directly elected (fixed term), Prime Minister appointed by President but responsible to legislature, dual executive with President handling foreign/defence and PM domestic policy, removal of PM by no-confidence, President by impeachment. A poor answer copies either pure model without addressing the tension between dual legitimacy (popular vs parliamentary).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A ______ executive system is one where the executive (Prime Minister and Council of Ministers) is drawn from, accountable to, and removable by the legislature (Lok Sabha), with a ceremonial head of state (President); a presidential executive system is one where the executive (President) is directly elected by the people for a fixed term, separate from the legislature, and not accountable to it through confidence votes.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are watching a news debate: in the UK, the Prime Minister faces hostile questions in ______ every Wednesday and can be voted out tomorrow; in the USA, the President serves a fixed four-year term regardless of Congress's mood.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Can distinguish parliamentary and presidential systems across five dimensions (origin, tenure, accountability, separation of powers, role of head of state) and explain why India's Constituent Assembly chose the parliamentary model despite its British colonial legacy.
